purpose: Ipratropium helps open up your airways so you can breathe more easily. It is commonly used for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic bronchitis, or emphysema. It can also be used to help with asthma in some cases, usually alongside other inhalers.
how_it_works: Your airways have tiny muscles around them that can tighten up and make it hard to breathe. Ipratropium works by blocking a signal in your body that causes those muscles to squeeze. When those muscles relax, your airways open wider and air can flow in and out much more freely.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth is the most common side effect. You may also notice a dry or irritated throat, cough, headache, dizziness, or an upset stomach. Some people experience blurred vision if the medication accidentally gets into their eyes, so be careful when using the inhaler.
warnings: Do not use this medication if you are allergic to ipratropium or atropine. Tell your doctor if you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or trouble urinating, as this medication can make those conditions worse. Avoid spraying it into your eyes. If your breathing suddenly gets much worse after using it, contact your doctor or seek emergency help right away. It is not a rescue inhaler for sudden breathing attacks — do not use it alone in an emergency.
typical_dosing: For COPD using the inhaler, a common dose is 2 puffs (34 mcg each) taken 4 times a day, roughly every 6 hours. Your doctor may adjust this based on your needs. If you are using the nasal spray for a runny nose, the usual dose is 2 sprays per nostril 2 to 3 times a day. Always follow the exact instructions your doctor or pharmacist gives you.
